extracted.intended_audience: educated readers in natural science and philosophy (scientists, physicians, and philosophically-minded public)
extracted.subtask_description: An essay examining the principal transcendental difficulties (the 'seven world-problems') that limit scientific understanding, arguing which are insoluble on purely mechanical grounds and discussing responses (e.g., Darwinian selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: The existence of matter and force
rubrics_metrics.description: The first difficulty is the existence of matter and force, and is in itself transcendental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author presents this as a fundamental, transcendental problem: the basic ontological fact that matter and force exist is not further analyzable by the methods of natural science; it stands as an initial, insoluble difficulty when considering the limits of our knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: The origin of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The second difficulty is the origin of motion. We see motion arise and cease; we can conceive matter at rest, and motion appears to be something casual to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues this is transcendent because, absent a supernatural impulse, there is no sufficient occasion for the first motion if matter is imagined at rest in infinite space; alternatively, positing eternal motion avoids explanation. Thus the origin of motion resists causal elucidation and is classed as transcendent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The origin of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The third difficulty is the origin of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly disagrees that this is transcendental: once matter moves, under suitable conditions life may arise by mechanical arrangements. Accepting a single supernatural act to create animated matter is enough; otherwise a mechanical origin of life is conceivable. Discussion references Pasteur and panspermy, Darwinian descent, and Leibnitz's idea of created animated matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: The apparently teleological arrangement of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth difficulty is offered by the apparently teleological arrangement of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organic laws of formation seem adaptive and inconsistent with the mechanical view unless matter was created with adaptive purpose. However, this difficulty is not absolutely transcendent: Darwin's doctrine of natural selection offers a plausible mechanism to explain adaptation and internal suitability of organisms without invoking final causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The origin of simple sensations (consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth difficulty is the origin of simple sensations, and is quite transcendent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay develops the argument that consciousness (even the simplest sensation) cannot be made comprehensible as the result of arrangements and movements of matter on mechanical grounds. The author invokes Leibnitz and related arguments: dividing matter into ever smaller particles or arranging them in any shape and motion will not produce sensation; astronomical knowledge of brain processes would not explain the origin of consciousness; proposed remedies (atom-souls, 'plastidule') are criticized as violating 'entia non creanda sinè necessitate' and failing to account for aggregated consciousness of the brain.
